**Sensitivity.** GeNIe is the cleanest: designate a target, and it **shades the whole network** — red nodes hold parameters that matter to the target's posterior, gray nodes have literally zero influence. Double-click a node's tornado icon for a ranked tornado diagram (green = positive, red = negative, default ±10% parameter spread, top-10 or all). Algorithm: Kjærulff & van der Gaag (2000) derivatives of posteriors w.r.t. parameters. The docs candidly admit "sensitivity analysis is essentially an art with few standard procedures." https://support.bayesfusion.com/docs/GeNIe/bn_sensitivitybn.html Also: value-of-information ranking of diagnostic tests, and Markov-blanket highlighting. https://www.bayesfusion.com/genie/

**Why they never went mainstream.** (a) **CPT elicitation burden** — table size is exponential in parent count; a binary node with *k* binary parents needs 2^k numbers, which is "costly and error-prone" and imposes a very high cognitive load per judgment. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12192095/ https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/risa.13772 Mitigations exist (Ranked Nodes Method, InterBeta, functional interpolation, noisy-OR) that cut 2^k to ~2k. (b) The **knowledge-acquisition bottleneck** is named as "one of the major drawbacks" and is the project-schedule bottleneck on large networks. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.3893 (c) No TensorFlow-equivalent ecosystem: tooling stayed expensive, desktop, Windows-first, academic-licensed. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.17025

**Transferable.** Distribution bars *inside* the node; click-a-state to set evidence with immediate global repropagation; named scenarios compared on one chart; red/gray sensitivity shading of the whole graph relative to a chosen target; VOI ranking → "which unknown should you resolve next." And the loud warning: **never make the user fill a 2^k table.** Use noisy-OR / ranked-node-style summaries with an escape hatch to the full table.

---

### 5. Squiggle & Guesstimate (Ozzie Gooen / QURI)

**Guesstimate** — a spreadsheet where every cell is a distribution. You type `5 to 9` for a 90% CI; it Monte-Carlos (default ~5k samples) and renders a **histogram inside the cell** plus mean and CI. Cells reference each other like a spreadsheet, correlations propagate through samples, and there's an "Analysis Mode" for sensitivity/scatter between any two cells. https://www.getguesstimate.com/ https://docs.getguesstimate.com/ https://docs.getguesstimate.com/docs/theory/monte_carlo_simulations **Squiggle** is the code-based successor: `x = 5 to 9` in a live playground, output pane re-renders distribution plots on every keystroke; distributions are first-class values and, crucially, *functions returning distributions* are the design goal. https://www.squiggle-language.com/ https://quri.substack.com/p/squiggle-overview-2020

**Does well.** `5 to 9` is the best uncertainty-input affordance ever designed — one token, no distribution-family choice, no parameter dialog. Sampling makes correlation and non-linear propagation free. Both are link-shareable and fork-friendly.

**Pitfalls.** Guesstimate "breaks down for larger or more demanding models"; Squiggle is "harder to understand than Guesstimate or Causal… which follows naturally from being code-based," and large Squiggle models have a **legibility problem** — output is a flat list in source order with no structure. https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/TsaRbCotCaWpcrt8F/squiggle-why-and-how-to-use-it Commercially it never found a market: Gooen concluded it was a niche space where growth meant pivoting away from the research mission, and QURI has since moved Guesstimate/Squiggle to maintenance mode. https://quantifieduncertainty.org/posts/announcing-squiggle-hub/

**Transferable.** The `a to b` literal; histogram-in-cell; sample-based propagation so joint effects are automatic; and the lesson that *text scales but stops being legible* — a graph UI over a sampling core is the unoccupied middle.

---

### 6. Causal-inference DAG tools — **relevance is limited; say so**

DAGitty (browser + R) lets you drag nodes, mark exposure/outcome/latent, and it live-computes **minimal sufficient adjustment sets**, open backdoor/frontdoor paths, instrumental variables, testable conditional independencies, and highlights paths as you hover. https://dagitty.net/ Causal Fusion implements sound-and-complete do-calculus identification and enumerates all valid adjustment sets. http://www.causalfusion.net DoWhy/PyWhy is a four-step library (model → identify → estimate → **refute**), notable for its refutation API that auto-tests assumptions; ShowWhy is its no-code GUI. https://www.pywhy.org/dowhy/

**Why mostly not transferable.** These are unquantified *identification* tools: nodes have no probabilities, edges have no strengths, and nothing propagates. Their question is "can this effect be estimated from data without bias," not "what happens if X." **Two things do transfer:** (a) the live-recomputed, path-highlighting response to changing a node's role — set a node to "adjusted" and every affected path restyles instantly; (b) DoWhy's **refutation step** as a stage in the UI — an explicit, named place where the model attacks its own assumptions.

---

### 7. Argument mapping: Rationale, Kialo, Arguman

**What.** Pro/con trees over a thesis. Kialo: claim at root, children tagged Pro/Con, recursively; users vote on impact; reading path is a breadcrumb down the tree. https://www.kialo-edu.com/ Rationale is instruction-oriented with scaffolded box templates; Arguman was an open-source pro/con/but-because graph (now largely dormant). https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/criticalthinking1234/chapter/introduction/

**Does well.** Structure is skimmable; anyone can join mid-debate and see where things stand; Rationale-style mapping does have measured critical-thinking gains in instructed settings. https://www.kialo-edu.com/research

**Why retention is low — the most useful set of failure modes here.**
- **Context loss in trees.** If C supports B and B supports A, there's no way to say "C supports B in general but is irrelevant *to A*." Comments that could express this are UI-marginal and don't feed the scoring. https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/g3odvaj8opqCF9egv/kialo-an-online-discussion-platform-that-attempts-to-support
- **Structural mismatch.** johnswentworth's critique: these tools picked the obvious data structure (a tree of claims) without analyzing what structure actually fits reasoning, so users "shoehorn" — friction comparable to prose, without prose's familiarity. https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/bHXpbf6jXc4bgyrrp/why-is-argument-mapping-not-more-common-in-ea-rationality
- **Learning curve as a new language**; **cold-start content quality**; **critical-mass chicken-and-egg**. (same thread)
- **Incentive asymmetry:** adding another Pro is cheap and scores points; engaging a critic's actual point is expensive — so trees inflate sideways rather than deepen. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10503-023-09626-5
- **Social flattening:** formalization "restricts social interaction," hurts perceived ease of use and collaboration, needs heavy moderation, and real conversation migrates off-platform. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12711
- **Representational gaps:** reductio, equivocation charges, logical analogies and mathematical arguments map badly. (Springer, above)

---

## Cross-cutting: the "change an input, see downstream effects" pattern catalogue

Ranked by what I'd steal for a probabilistic causal-chain builder:

1. **Slider-per-parameter with inline sparklines on the nodes themselves** (Vensim SyntheSim) — no modal, no side panel, no run button. The model diagram *is* the dashboard.
2. **Ghosted baseline under the live curve** (SyntheSim) — before/after diffing comes free, and it's what makes scrubbing interpretable rather than just wiggly.
3. **Distribution rendered inside the node** (Netica/GeNIe bars; Guesstimate histogram-in-cell) — the graph carries its own numbers; no hover, no drill-down.
4. **Click-a-state to clamp evidence, everything repropagates instantly** (all BN GUIs) — the closest existing analogue to "assume this event happened; re-price the chain."
5. **Whole-graph sensitivity shading against a chosen target** (GeNIe red/gray) — answers "which of these 40 nodes actually matters to my question" at a glance, before any tornado chart.
6. **Tornado chart as the second-level drill** (GeNIe, BayesiaLab) — ranked, signed, with a stated perturbation size (±10%).
7. **Named scenarios overlaid on one chart** (AgenaRisk) — not tabs you flip between; simultaneous overlay.
8. **VOI / next-best-question ranking** (BayesiaLab Adaptive Questionnaire, GeNIe diagnosis) — turns a static model into a workflow: *go resolve this uncertainty next.*
9. **Animated pulse traversal with visible latency** (Loopy) — the only one that makes propagation felt rather than inferred; cheap, and enormously good for comprehension of chains.
10. **Backward causal tracing as navigation** (Vensim) — click an outcome, walk up its causes, each with its own behavior.
11. **`5 to 9` range literal** (Guesstimate/Squiggle) — the lowest-friction uncertainty input known.
12. **Views over one dataset + rule-based decoration** (Kumu) — how you keep a big causal graph readable.

And the four failure modes to design against, in order of likelihood: **underspecified diagrams that animate anyway** (Loopy's multi-loop problem) — if you animate propagation, the semantics must be real or explicitly labelled as illustrative; **2^k elicitation** (BN CPTs) — default to noisy-OR/ranked-node summaries; **proof-by-intimidation** (Kumu) — thorough-looking graphs get believed, so render confidence and provenance as loudly as structure; and **context loss + pro-side inflation** (Kialo) — a chain where each link's strength is judged out of context, and where adding supporting links is cheaper than attacking them, will drift confidently wrong.

## Summary

**The central claim:** the finance layer lives or dies on one identity — `Edge = Σ(pₛ − qₛ)·Sₛ`. The conditional move is not the edge; disagreement with the market is. Set your probabilities equal to the market's and edge must read zero no matter how violent the event. A tool without a "what's already priced in" column is a narrative generator in a finance costume.

**Getting *q* cheaply:** Polymarket/Kalshi public keyless endpoints (Brier ~0.19, superforecaster-class); call-spread arithmetic instead of spline-fitted Breeden-Litzenberger (`e^{rT}(C(K₁)−C(K₂))/(K₂−K₁)` brackets the digital probability); ATM straddle/spot as the market's expected absolute move (1σ ≈ 1.25× that); FedWatch-style day-weighted futures arithmetic. Always badge option-derived numbers as risk-neutral.

**Magnitudes from literature, not vibes:** oil elasticities ~0.08 supply / −0.08 demand (Caldara-Cavallo-Iacoviello) means a 1% supply loss ≈ 10% price move; Kilian's finding that flow-supply shocks historically moved price *less* than demand shocks; free GPR index; a ~50-line event-study function over free bars.

**Biggest technical trap:** P(terminal below stop) ≠ P(stop hit) — ~2× apart for a driftless process. Gave the closed-form barrier formula plus a 1k-path MC for the two-barrier case.

**Sizing:** full Kelly on LLM probabilities is reckless (MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba); make risk-budget sizing primary, Kelly secondary, capped at ¼, computed at *p_low*.

**Best-fit feature:** reverse stress testing — the brief literally describes the regulatory definition. Enumerate paths hitting the stop, rank by probability, extract the node common to the worst ones.

Deliverables: a 6-formula minimal core with concrete data fields, 8 rigor traps each with a falsifiable test (a reviewer can run all 8 in 20 minutes), and a don't-build list (no optimizer, no backtester, no covariance model, no SVI fitting).</result>

The quant-finance researcher is done, and its report is at `plans/review2/research-B-quant-finance.md`. The other two researchers and all five auditors are still running.

The report agrees with my first pass on the inverse query and on position sizing. It also adds two points I will carry into the synthesis:

- **Edge is disagreement with the market.** The report's central formula is `Edge = Σ(pₛ − qₛ)·Sₛ`, where `p` is the tool's probability for scenario *s*, `q` is the market's, and `S` is the size of the price move in that scenario. If the tool's probabilities equal the market's, the edge must be zero however large the event is. I'll check the project against this once the finance audit lands: is there a priced-in column, and is divergence computed anywhere?
- **The chance of touching a stop is not the chance of finishing below it.** For a price with no drift, the chance of hitting the stop at some point is roughly twice the chance of ending below it. Any stop or target feature has to account for this or state its approximation.

The report also notes that the brief's stop-loss sentence matches the regulatory definition of reverse stress testing. That supports treating it as a query from a price level back to the events that reach it, as flagged earlier.

I'll wait for the remaining agents before writing the synthesis or asking you questions.

# Design-review briefing: conditional forecasting, causal-chain UX, explorables, node canvases, scenario diffs

## A) Metaculus question structure

**Anatomy.** A Metaculus question is a contract with four prose slots plus dates: **title**, **background**, **resolution criteria**, **fine print**, and **open / close / resolve dates**. The load-bearing distinction is stated flatly in the FAQ: *"Only the resolution criteria is relevant for resolving a question; the background section is intended only to provide potentially useful information and context for forecasters. In a well-specified question, the resolution criteria should stand on its own as a set of self-contained instructions for resolving the question... the information in the resolution criteria supersedes conflicting information in the background material."* ([FAQ](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/), source: [`faq/page.tsx`](https://github.com/Metaculus/metaculus/blob/main/front_end/src/app/(main)/faq/page.tsx))

Fine print exists purely as a readability valve: *"Delegate the boring stuff to the fine-print. In some cases, the resolution criteria might become quite detailed and involved. To keep questions streamlined, it can be convenient to relegate some of the gory details to the fine-print."* ([question-writing guidelines](https://www.metaculus.com/question-writing/)). This is the key design lesson: **the operationalization is the artifact**, and the UI deliberately splits it into a short authoritative spine (resolution criteria) plus a collapsible tail (fine print) plus non-binding context (background). Metaculus also runs a formal [Question Approval Checklist](https://www.metaculus.com/help/question-checklist/) — questions are reviewed before going live, because an ambiguous criterion poisons every forecast attached to it and forces **annulment**.

**Question Groups.** *"Question groups are sets of closely related questions or question outcomes all collected on a single page. Forecasters can predict quickly and efficiently on these interconnected outcomes, confident that they are keeping all of their predictions internally consistent."* The stated UX payoff: *"A question group collecting multiple binary questions on a limited set of outcomes or on mutually exclusive outcomes makes it easier to see which forecasts are in tension with each other."* Groups are explicitly distinguished from Multiple Choice: MC is **one** question, options mutually exclusive and exhaustive, probabilities sum to 100%, **one score**; a Group is *n* independent questions sharing a page and *n* scores.

**Conditional Pairs — the important one.** *"A Conditional Pair is a special type of Question Group that elicits conditional probabilities. Each Conditional Pair sits between a Parent Question and a Child Question. Both Parent and Child must be existing Metaculus Binary Questions."* It asks two Conditionals: *"If the Parent resolves Yes, how will the Child resolve? If the Parent resolves No, how will the Child resolve?"*

Two distinct visual treatments, which is directly relevant to your canvas:
1. **Forecasting interface** — a **table**: the two conditionals presented *"next to each other for convenience"* (screenshots: `cdn.metaculus.com/conditional_faq_2.jpg`, `conditional_faq_3.jpg`).
2. **Feed tile** — *"in the feeds, each possible outcome of the Parent is an arrow, and each conditional probability is a bar."* So the if/then arrow is a **two-branch fork glyph**: one node (Parent) → two labelled arrows (if Yes / if No) → two bars (Child probability under each branch). Screenshot: `cdn.metaculus.com/conditional_faq_1.jpg`. Metaculus later shipped **conditional continuous** questions where the Child is numeric — the UI becomes **IF YES / IF NO buttons** that each open a distribution editor ([EA Forum announcement](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/jhNicnLKW6apH6TES/metaculus-introduces-conditional-continuous-questions-to)). They also had to fix embed rendering with *"responsive branch charts"* ([PR #5186](https://github.com/Metaculus/metaculus/pull/5186)) — branch diagrams are genuinely hard to make responsive.

**Lifecycle:** *"When the Parent resolves Yes, the 'if No' Conditional is Annulled (and vice versa). When the Child resolves, the Conditional that was not annulled resolves to the same value."* The dead branch is **not scored** — it does not count against you. That is a crucial affordance for a causal-chain UI: counterfactual branches must be visibly *retired*, not silently deleted or penalized.

**Why built.** Per the launch post: *"Two forecasters could have the same forecasts... while having very different mental models of their relationship."* Conditional pairs make implicit causal models **explicit, discussable and scoreable**, and quantify policy/event impact. The difference between the two branches *is* the estimated causal effect. ([LessWrong](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/nQhmiKeYPvFaEZfWc/metaculus-introduces-new-conditional-pair-forecast-questions), [EA Forum](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/qELZknyx8eBg7HskH/metaculus-introduces-new-conditional-pair-forecast-questions), [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZvZeA0qvZXg)). Launch examples were causal chains: compute restrictions → AI timelines; Chinese GDP → US-China conflict; Ukraine ceasefire → future Russian conflict.

**Community Prediction & scoring.** The CP is *"a consensus of recent forecaster predictions... designed to respond to big changes in forecaster opinion while still being fairly insensitive to outliers"* — a **recency-weighted median** (weight ∝ position in the recency ordering), renormalized for multiple choice. Legacy Brier numbers: MP 0.107 vs CP 0.108 for 2021 resolutions; **lower is better**. Modern scoring is log-score-derived ([Scores FAQ](https://www.metaculus.com/help/scores-faq/)):
- **Log score** = ln(p(outcome)); for continuous, ln(pdf(outcome)) with a uniform 0.01 added to every pdf to cap extremes. Always negative for binary/MC — *"This has proved unintuitive, which is one reason why Metaculus uses the Baseline and Peer scores."*
- **Baseline score**: log score rescaled against a chance baseline (50% binary, 1/N for MC, uniform for continuous). 0 = chance, +100 = perfect. Empirically, median binary Baseline ≈ **+17**, mean ≈ +13; worst possible ≈ **-897**.
- **Peer score**: vs. other forecasters; **Spot score**: a single snapshot rather than time-averaged (coverage 100% or 0%); **Coverage**: fraction of question lifetime you held a live forecast.
- The asymmetry lesson worth stealing for UI copy: going 99% → 99.9% gains +0.009 if right, costs **-2.3** if wrong.

## B) Prediction markets as causal-chain UX

**Polymarket** has no conditional primitive. Its model is **Series → Events → Markets**, where a market is a binary $1/$0 contract and an "event" is a folder of related binaries ([docs](https://docs.polymarket.us/concepts/events-and-markets)). Multi-outcome races are *assembled* from binaries grouped under one event with implied probabilities shown as a proportional bar. Causality is expressed only by **adjacency** (related markets on one page) — never by an edge.

**Manifold** has shipped three generations of multiple-choice mechanism: n-outcome dynamic parimutuel (good liquidity, no fixed payouts), n-outcome CPMM (degraded when an option went extreme), and the current design ([Multiple Choice Markets](https://news.manifold.markets/p/multiple-choice-markets)). "Conditional markets" on Manifold are **a social convention, not a feature** — a [conditional-markets topic page](https://manifold.markets/topic/conditional-markets) of hand-written "If X, then Y?" markets, plus bounties encouraging users to create Biden/Trump conditional pairs manually ([example](https://manifold.markets/ManifoldPolitics/make-markets-about-what-will-happen)). Native dependent/partial resolution is an open request forecast [not before 2028](https://manifold.markets/FlorisvanDoorn/when-will-manifold-markets-allow-us). **Takeaway: the conditional-pair primitive is a genuine gap in the market UIs; Metaculus is the only one with first-class support.**

**What traders want to see** ([prediction-market design patterns guide](https://avark.agency/learn/prediction-market-design-patterns)): a three-layer **progressive disclosure** stack — (1) card: event, probability, one action; (2) probability timeline chart, trade history, **resolution criteria**; (3) order book, depth, full spec. Dual encoding of price-as-probability ("72¢"), horizontal proportional bars for multi-outcome with hover exact values, **animated 200-300ms number transitions** rather than jumps, desaturated green/red direction, and explicit **resolution-source / oracle transparency** as a trust signal.

## C) Explorables & immediate feedback

Bret Victor, [Explorable Explanations](https://worrydream.com/ExplorableExplanations/): the goal is turning prose from *"information to be consumed"* into *"an environment to think in."* Three patterns: **reactive documents** (Tangle — scrub an assumption inline, the argument's numbers update), **explorable examples** (manipulate parameters against multiple simultaneous representations), **contextual information** (in-place lookup). Key line: *"By watching the result change as we adjust parameters, we can develop an intuition for the system's behavior."*

[Ladder of Abstraction](https://worrydream.com/LadderOfAbstraction/): *"A designer needs direct, interactive control over the independent variables of the system."* The rungs — interactive control → abstracting over time (show the whole trajectory, not one instant) → range visualization (overlay many trajectories) → **small multiples** → stepping back down to a concrete instance. The core move is **"one particular" vs "all possible"**: a single run tells you nothing; the family of runs is the object of understanding.

[Learnable Programming](https://worrydream.com/LearnableProgramming/) gives the most directly actionable checklist: read the vocabulary / follow the flow / see the state / create by reacting / create by abstracting. Requirements: **"Show the data"** — *"the number one thing you can do... The entire purpose of code is to manipulate data, and we never see the data."* **"All state must be eliminated or shown."** Make flow visible; **make time tangible** (scrub backwards and forwards, compare moments).

Nicky Case adds pedagogy over mechanics: [Explorable Explanations](https://blog.ncase.me/explorable-explanations/) and [4 More Design Patterns](https://blog.ncase.me/explorable-explanations-4-more-design-patterns/) — **Puzzle It Out**, **Place Your Bets!** (elicit a prediction *before* revealing the answer — cognitive conflict makes the answer land; this is exactly your forecasting affordance doubling as a teaching device), **Role Play**, **Sandbox Mode** (end in an unconstrained playground). Sequencing advice: motivate the question, start with an experience, narrative flow ("X therefore Y, but Z"), guided → self-directed. Also [How I Make Explorable Explanations](https://blog.ncase.me/how-i-make-an-explorable-explanation/) and the [awesome-explorables list](https://github.com/blob42/awesome-explorables).

**What makes "change a thing, see the effect" feel great:** sub-100ms loop, no commit/apply step, the changed input stays visible next to the changed output, the *previous* value remains on screen as a ghost, and the effect is shown across the whole range, not just at the new point.

## D) Node canvas libraries & failure modes

**React Flow / xyflow** ([reactflow.dev](https://reactflow.dev/learn/concepts/introduction)) gives you free: viewport pan/zoom, nodes with x/y, **handles** as attachment points, four edge types (`default` bezier, `smoothstep`, `step`, `straight`) as styleable SVG paths, multi-select (Meta/Ctrl individual, Shift box), and plugin components **Background, Controls, MiniMap, NodeToolbar, NodeResizer, EdgeLabelRenderer, EdgeToolbar, Panel, ViewportPortal**. `EdgeLabelRenderer` is the one to note for conditional branch labels ("if Yes" / "if No") — it renders labels in a DOM layer above edges so they stay crisp and clickable.

**Auto-layout** ([layouting docs](https://reactflow.dev/learn/layouting/layouting)): **dagre** — *"minimal configuration options and a focus on speed over choosing the most optimal layout"*, best for trees, known bug with sub-flows connected externally; **d3-hierarchy** — single-root trees only, assumes uniform node size (bad for heterogeneous nodes); **d3-force** — organic, non-tree, but *"computing the force layout every render forever is going to incur a big performance hit"*; **ELK.js** — *"certainly the most configurable option available, but it's also the most complicated"*, async, real edge routing, Java-flavored docs. **For a conditional/causal DAG, ELK layered (or dagre if you want it cheap) is the right call**, with a fixed left→right rank direction.

**Classic failures**, well documented in the Unreal Blueprint literature ([Avoiding blueprint spaghetti](https://jdn.dev/avoiding-blueprint-spaghetti/), [10 techniques](https://uhiyama-lab.com/en/notes/ue/blueprint-spaghetti-code-prevention-techniques/), [Epic docs](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/nodes-in-unreal-engine), [Dan MacKinlay on patchers](https://danmackinlay.name/notebook/patchers.html)): edge spaghetti and crossing links where *"it's easy to completely mistake what goes where"*; node soup with no reading order; layout thrash when auto-layout re-runs and everything jumps. Mitigations that actually work: **enforce one-way left-to-right flow**, comment boxes / groups as visual chapters, reroute nodes, node alignment, aggressive decomposition into small subgraphs, and limiting how much graph is on screen at once. Crossing minimization is NP-hard — you will never get a perfect layout, so **stability matters more than optimality**: animate layout changes, preserve user-pinned positions, and never reflow the whole canvas on a small edit.

**"Where do I start reading"** is answered by Shneiderman's 1996 mantra, *"Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand"* ([The Eyes Have It](http://www.ifp.illinois.edu/nabhcs/abstracts/shneiderman.html), [summary](https://jtr13.github.io/cc21/ben-shneidermans-visualization-mantra.html)) plus focus+context / overview+detail. Concretely: a minimap for overview, an explicit entry node or numbered path bar, collapsed node bodies at low zoom that expand with density (semantic zoom), edge labels only near focus, and an inspector panel for details rather than fat nodes.

**Library choice:** React Flow is *"the component that's closest to supporting structured node-based diagramming"*; Excalidraw is MIT and free forever; **tldraw's SDK since 4.0 (Sept 2025) requires a paid commercial license (~$6,000/yr) after a 100-day trial** ([comparison](https://tryquickdraw.com/blog/tldraw-vs-excalidraw-vs-quickdraw)) — a real procurement consideration. [Rete.js](https://retejs.org/docs/) is the one that ships an actual **execution engine** (dataflow *and* control flow, combinable in one graph) with framework-agnostic rendering; LiteGraph.js is older and much less used (~1.6k weekly downloads vs Rete's ~71k). xyflow maintains [awesome-node-based-uis](https://github.com/xyflow/awesome-node-based-uis).

## E) Scenario / diff UX: world A vs world B

**Tornado diagrams** are the canonical "what moves the outcome" view: a bar chart of the delta between low-case and base and high-case and base for each input, **sorted by absolute impact**, widest at top ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_diagram), [Ed Bodmer](https://edbodmer.com/fundamentals-of-creating-a-tornado-diagram-and-creating-sensitivity-analysis/), [Decision Frameworks](https://decisionframeworks.com/blog/how-to-build-and-interpret-tornado-diagrams-for-sensitivity-analysis), [Wiley ch. 18](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781118957394.ch18)). It is a **summary of many one-way sensitivities**, each varied alone with others held at base. Practical rule from the field: **7-12 bars is optimal; under 5 doesn't justify the format, over 15 is clutter** — with 30+ inputs, compute all and display only the top 10-12 ([Deckary](https://deckary.com/blog/tornado-chart-powerpoint)). Note the direct structural analogy: a tornado bar *is* the Metaculus conditional-pair spread (P(child | parent Yes) − P(child | parent No)), sorted.

**Waterfall charts** answer the complementary question — not "which input matters" but "how did we get from base to this case", decomposing the bridge contribution by contribution ([SumProduct](https://sumproduct.com/thought/tornado-charts/)). Standard practice is to pair them: tornado on the summary for *which variables matter*, sensitivity tables in the appendix for the top 2-3, and named scenario analysis (Bull / Base / Bear) for specific strategic cases.

**Finance scenario tooling worth citing.** The Fed publishes **baseline vs severely adverse** macro scenarios as paired variable paths ([2025 scenarios PDF](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/2025-stress-test-scenarios-20250205.pdf)). The best interactive example is the **Minneapolis Fed large-bank stress test tool** ([link](https://www.minneapolisfed.org/banking/financial-studies-and-community-banking/run-your-own-stress-test-on-large-banks)): the user picks a bank (or "22 Firm total"), picks a named preset scenario (Moderate recession / Extreme recession / Rising rates, with **Select all** for overlay), and toggles policy levers (historical payouts vs no payout; remove SCB). Output is projected capital ratios over nine quarters with a **red required-capital threshold line** — a persistent reference line is the cheapest possible "world A" anchor. Eight small-multiple charts show the macro variable paths underneath, so the cause and the consequence are on screen together. That combination — **preset scenarios + a few toggles + overlaid trajectories + a fixed threshold + small multiples of the drivers** — is a directly copyable pattern.

**Diff idioms and when each wins.** Superimposed **before/after sliders** align two states pixel-for-pixel so subtle changes pop; **fade/opacity crossfade** beats a hard divider for spotting tone or alignment shifts; **side-by-side** wins when you need to compare proportions rather than find differences ([overview](https://scanly.co/image-comparison), [technique roundup](https://www.hongkiat.com/blog/js-image-comparison-sliders/)). For abstract data the equivalents are **ghost overlays** (scenario B drawn over a greyed scenario A on the same axes — traders explicitly want *"to overlay two different scenarios on the same chart, so that they can visually compare strategies"*, [issue](https://github.com/greg-motion-dev/interest-ing/issues/13)), **pinned scenario comparison** (A stays docked while you manipulate B), and **small multiples** per Victor's ladder. Ann Emery catalogues four before/after framings including plotting the **delta** directly rather than both levels ([4 Ideas for Visualizing Before-After Comparisons](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/4-ideas-visualizing-before-after-comparisons-ann-k-emery)).

## Synthesis for your canvas

The three strongest transferable ideas: (1) **Metaculus's fork glyph** — one node, two labelled arrows, two bars — is the minimal, proven visual for "if A then B / if not-A then B", and the *annul-don't-delete* rule for the dead branch is as important as the glyph. (2) **The gap between the two branches is the causal claim**, which means the diff view (tornado-sorted branch spreads) is the payoff screen, not a side panel. (3) **Victor's "show the data / no hidden state / make time tangible" plus Shneiderman's overview→zoom→details-on-demand** resolve the node-soup problem: keep nodes thin, put detail in an inspector, label edges only in focus, and make layout changes animate rather than teleport.</result>

Also [How I Make Explorable Explanations](https://blog.ncase.me/how-i-make-an-explorable-explanation/) and the [awesome-explorables list](https://github.com/blob42/awesome-explorables).

**What makes "change a thing, see the effect" feel great:** sub-100ms loop, no commit/apply step, the changed input stays visible next to the changed output, the *previous* value remains on screen as a ghost, and the effect is shown across the whole range, not just at the new point.

## D) Node canvas libraries & failure modes

**React Flow / xyflow** ([reactflow.dev](https://reactflow.dev/learn/concepts/introduction)) gives you free: viewport pan/zoom, nodes with x/y, **handles** as attachment points, four edge types (`default` bezier, `smoothstep`, `step`, `straight`) as styleable SVG paths, multi-select (Meta/Ctrl individual, Shift box), and plugin components **Background, Controls, MiniMap, NodeToolbar, NodeResizer, EdgeLabelRenderer, EdgeToolbar, Panel, ViewportPortal**. `EdgeLabelRenderer` is the one to note for conditional branch labels ("if Yes" / "if No") — it renders labels in a DOM layer above edges so they stay crisp and clickable.

**Auto-layout** ([layouting docs](https://reactflow.dev/learn/layouting/layouting)): **dagre** — *"minimal configuration options and a focus on speed over choosing the most optimal layout"*, best for trees, known bug with sub-flows connected externally; **d3-hierarchy** — single-root trees only, assumes uniform node size (bad for heterogeneous nodes); **d3-force** — organic, non-tree, but *"computing the force layout every render forever is going to incur a big performance hit"*; **ELK.js** — *"certainly the most configurable option available, but it's also the most complicated"*, async, real edge routing, Java-flavored docs. **For a conditional/causal DAG, ELK layered (or dagre if you want it cheap) is the right call**, with a fixed left→right rank direction.

**Classic failures**, well documented in the Unreal Blueprint literature ([Avoiding blueprint spaghetti](https://jdn.dev/avoiding-blueprint-spaghetti/), [10 techniques](https://uhiyama-lab.com/en/notes/ue/blueprint-spaghetti-code-prevention-techniques/), [Epic docs](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/nodes-in-unreal-engine), [Dan MacKinlay on patchers](https://danmackinlay.name/notebook/patchers.html)): edge spaghetti and crossing links where *"it's easy to completely mistake what goes where"*; node soup with no reading order; layout thrash when auto-layout re-runs and everything jumps. Mitigations that actually work: **enforce one-way left-to-right flow**, comment boxes / groups as visual chapters, reroute nodes, node alignment, aggressive decomposition into small subgraphs, and limiting how much graph is on screen at once. Crossing minimization is NP-hard — you will never get a perfect layout, so **stability matters more than optimality**: animate layout changes, preserve user-pinned positions, and never reflow the whole canvas on a small edit.

**"Where do I start reading"** is answered by Shneiderman's 1996 mantra, *"Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand"* ([The Eyes Have It](http://www.ifp.illinois.edu/nabhcs/abstracts/shneiderman.html), [summary](https://jtr13.github.io/cc21/ben-shneidermans-visualization-mantra.html)) plus focus+context / overview+detail. Concretely: a minimap for overview, an explicit entry node or numbered path bar, collapsed node bodies at low zoom that expand with density (semantic zoom), edge labels only near focus, and an inspector panel for details rather than fat nodes.

**Library choice:** React Flow is *"the component that's closest to supporting structured node-based diagramming"*; Excalidraw is MIT and free forever; **tldraw's SDK since 4.0 (Sept 2025) requires a paid commercial license (~$6,000/yr) after a 100-day trial** ([comparison](https://tryquickdraw.com/blog/tldraw-vs-excalidraw-vs-quickdraw)) — a real procurement consideration. [Rete.js](https://retejs.org/docs/) is the one that ships an actual **execution engine** (dataflow *and* control flow, combinable in one graph) with framework-agnostic rendering; LiteGraph.js is older and much less used (~1.6k weekly downloads vs Rete's ~71k). xyflow maintains [awesome-node-based-uis](https://github.com/xyflow/awesome-node-based-uis).

## E) Scenario / diff UX: world A vs world B

**Tornado diagrams** are the canonical "what moves the outcome" view: a bar chart of the delta between low-case and base and high-case and base for each input, **sorted by absolute impact**, widest at top ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_diagram), [Ed Bodmer](https://edbodmer.com/fundamentals-of-creating-a-tornado-diagram-and-creating-sensitivity-analysis/), [Decision Frameworks](https://decisionframeworks.com/blog/how-to-build-and-interpret-tornado-diagrams-for-sensitivity-analysis), [Wiley ch. 18](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781118957394.ch18)). It is a **summary of many one-way sensitivities**, each varied alone with others held at base. Practical rule from the field: **7-12 bars is optimal; under 5 doesn't justify the format, over 15 is clutter** — with 30+ inputs, compute all and display only the top 10-12 ([Deckary](https://deckary.com/blog/tornado-chart-powerpoint)). Note the direct structural analogy: a tornado bar *is* the Metaculus conditional-pair spread (P(child | parent Yes) − P(child | parent No)), sorted.

**Waterfall charts** answer the complementary question — not "which input matters" but "how did we get from base to this case", decomposing the bridge contribution by contribution ([SumProduct](https://sumproduct.com/thought/tornado-charts/)). Standard practice is to pair them: tornado on the summary for *which variables matter*, sensitivity tables in the appendix for the top 2-3, and named scenario analysis (Bull / Base / Bear) for specific strategic cases.

**Finance scenario tooling worth citing.** The Fed publishes **baseline vs severely adverse** macro scenarios as paired variable paths ([2025 scenarios PDF](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/2025-stress-test-scenarios-20250205.pdf)). The best interactive example is the **Minneapolis Fed large-bank stress test tool** ([link](https://www.minneapolisfed.org/banking/financial-studies-and-community-banking/run-your-own-stress-test-on-large-banks)): the user picks a bank (or "22 Firm total"), picks a named preset scenario (Moderate recession / Extreme recession / Rising rates, with **Select all** for overlay), and toggles policy levers (historical payouts vs no payout; remove SCB). Output is projected capital ratios over nine quarters with a **red required-capital threshold line** — a persistent reference line is the cheapest possible "world A" anchor. Eight small-multiple charts show the macro variable paths underneath, so the cause and the consequence are on screen together. That combination — **preset scenarios + a few toggles + overlaid trajectories + a fixed threshold + small multiples of the drivers** — is a directly copyable pattern.

**Diff idioms and when each wins.** Superimposed **before/after sliders** align two states pixel-for-pixel so subtle changes pop; **fade/opacity crossfade** beats a hard divider for spotting tone or alignment shifts; **side-by-side** wins when you need to compare proportions rather than find differences ([overview](https://scanly.co/image-comparison), [technique roundup](https://www.hongkiat.com/blog/js-image-comparison-sliders/)). For abstract data the equivalents are **ghost overlays** (scenario B drawn over a greyed scenario A on the same axes — traders explicitly want *"to overlay two different scenarios on the same chart, so that they can visually compare strategies"*, [issue](https://github.com/greg-motion-dev/interest-ing/issues/13)), **pinned scenario comparison** (A stays docked while you manipulate B), and **small multiples** per Victor's ladder. Ann Emery catalogues four before/after framings including plotting the **delta** directly rather than both levels ([4 Ideas for Visualizing Before-After Comparisons](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/4-ideas-visualizing-before-after-comparisons-ann-k-emery)).

## Synthesis for your canvas

The three strongest transferable ideas: (1) **Metaculus's fork glyph** — one node, two labelled arrows, two bars — is the minimal, proven visual for "if A then B / if not-A then B", and the *annul-don't-delete* rule for the dead branch is as important as the glyph. (2) **The gap between the two branches is the causal claim**, which means the diff view (tornado-sorted branch spreads) is the payoff screen, not a side panel. ## 2. The "analytic" oracle is semi-circular

`test_range_matches_analytic_first_order_on_fixture` — `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/tests/unit/domain/test_propagation.py:745`

The slopes are obtained by finite-differencing **the engine itself** (6 more `propagate` calls), not by an independent model:

```python
# :771-776
up   = propagate(_frozen(HORMUZ, source,  step), (), as_of=FIXTURE_DATE, seed=SEED, **FULL)
down = propagate(_frozen(HORMUZ, source, -step), (), as_of=FIXTURE_DATE, seed=SEED, **FULL)
slope[target][source] = (
    _log_odds(up.beliefs[target].p) - _log_odds(down.beliefs[target].p)
) / (2.0 * step)
```

And the half-widths it feeds in (`:760-766`) re-derive the engine's own prior parameterisation, constant included:

```python
halves = {one.id: ((_log_odds(one.prior.p) - _log_odds(one.prior.lo)) / 1.2816,
                   (_log_odds(one.prior.hi) - _log_odds(one.prior.p)) / 1.2816) ...}
```

That is character-for-character `_fitted_halves` in `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/src/katalyst/domain/propagation.py:1104-1107` (`(middle - bottom) / NINETIETH_PERCENTILE`, with `NINETIETH_PERCENTILE = 1.2816` at `:107`). The centre also comes from the engine (`middle = _log_odds(middles.beliefs[target].p)`, `:791`).

**What it genuinely tests:** only the *uncertainty-combination step* — MC 10th/90th weighted percentile of variance-shrunk per-version values (`propagation.py:1399-1410`) vs. a root-sum-square delta-method linearisation. Those two are independent of each other.

**What it cannot catch:** any error in the forward causal arithmetic (strength/lag/shape/mode composition, collider handling, conditioning). Such a bug perturbs `up`, `down`, `middles` and `sampled` identically and cancels out of both sides of the assertion. The docstring's claim of "two independent methods" (`:746`) and the module header's "a second, independent method" (`:17`) overstate it.

**The one genuinely independent oracle** is `test_the_series_reads_the_arithmetic_written_in_the_chapter` (`:840`), which hand-computes from the link parameters alone:

## 3. `observe` vs. exact Bayes: no such test exists

`test_observe_may_update_ancestors` — `test_propagation.py:457-478`, in full:

```python
@given(st.data())
@many
def test_observe_may_update_ancestors(data: st.DataObject) -> None:
    """Learning something reaches back into what caused it, which supposing never does.
    ...That is a *capability* claim, so the map is filtered to ones where a
    cause could move at all."""
    graph = data.draw(graphs())
    target = data.draw(st.sampled_from([one.id for one in graph.propositions]))
    causes = _causes_of(graph, target)
    assume(causes)
    claims = {one.id: one for one in graph.propositions}
    assume(0.05 < claims[target].prior.p < 0.95)
    assume(any(0.0 < claims[one].prior.p < 1.0 for one in causes))

    base = _folded(graph)
    learned = _folded(graph, Observe(target=target, value=True))

    assert any(learned.beliefs[one] != base.beliefs[one] for one in causes)
```

It asserts **"something changed"** — an existential `!=` over a Belief dataclass, at `SMALL = {"versions": 16, "worlds": 4}` (`:64`). No direction, no magnitude, no sign. Observing a positively-linked cause could *lower* its ancestor's probability and this passes. The docstring is candid ("a *capability* claim"), but it is the only ancestor-update test in the file.

The only exact-conditioning check is degenerate: `test_an_observation_forces_the_claim_it_names` (`:1036`) asserts the observed node itself reads exactly `{1.0}` or `{0.0}`. Repo-wide grep for `bayes|Bayes|itertools.product|brute|enumerat|oracle` over `tests/` returns **zero** hits for a posterior oracle.

**Missing entirely:** law of total probability, Bayes consistency, conditional independence (d-separation as a *numeric* statement), convergence to an analytic value as `versions → ∞`, and any exact enumeration. With `graphs()` capped at 8 nodes, a 2^8 = 256-world exact enumeration oracle would be cheap and is the obvious gap.

## 2. The "analytic" oracle is semi-circular

`test_range_matches_analytic_first_order_on_fixture` — `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/tests/unit/domain/test_propagation.py:745`

The slopes are obtained by finite-differencing **the engine itself** (6 more `propagate` calls), not by an independent model:

```python
# :771-776
up   = propagate(_frozen(HORMUZ, source,  step), (), as_of=FIXTURE_DATE, seed=SEED, **FULL)
down = propagate(_frozen(HORMUZ, source, -step), (), as_of=FIXTURE_DATE, seed=SEED, **FULL)
slope[target][source] = (
    _log_odds(up.beliefs[target].p) - _log_odds(down.beliefs[target].p)
) / (2.0 * step)
```

And the half-widths it feeds in (`:760-766`) re-derive the engine's own prior parameterisation, constant included:

```python
halves = {one.id: ((_log_odds(one.prior.p) - _log_odds(one.prior.lo)) / 1.2816,
                   (_log_odds(one.prior.hi) - _log_odds(one.prior.p)) / 1.2816) ...}
```

That is character-for-character `_fitted_halves` in `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/src/katalyst/domain/propagation.py:1104-1107` (`(middle - bottom) / NINETIETH_PERCENTILE`, with `NINETIETH_PERCENTILE = 1.2816` at `:107`). The centre also comes from the engine (`middle = _log_odds(middles.beliefs[target].p)`, `:791`).

**What it genuinely tests:** only the *uncertainty-combination step* — MC 10th/90th weighted percentile of variance-shrunk per-version values (`propagation.py:1399-1410`) vs. a root-sum-square delta-method linearisation. Those two are independent of each other.

**What it cannot catch:** any error in the forward causal arithmetic (strength/lag/shape/mode composition, collider handling, conditioning). Such a bug perturbs `up`, `down`, `middles` and `sampled` identically and cancels out of both sides of the assertion. The docstring's claim of "two independent methods" (`:746`) and the module header's "a second, independent method" (`:17`) overstate it.

**The one genuinely independent oracle** is `test_the_series_reads_the_arithmetic_written_in_the_chapter` (`:840`), which hand-computes from the link parameters alone:
```python
# :857-858
by_hand_day_zero = _likelihood(_log_odds(0.28) - 2.4)
by_hand_day_ten  = _likelihood(_log_odds(0.28) - 1.2)
```
Scope: 2 nodes, 1 arrow, one impulse, tolerance 0.01. No multi-parent, no chain, no conditioning.

`test_observe_may_update_ancestors` — `test_propagation.py:457-478`, in full:

```python
@given(st.data())
@many
def test_observe_may_update_ancestors(data: st.DataObject) -> None:
    """Learning something reaches back into what caused it, which supposing never does.
    ...That is a *capability* claim, so the map is filtered to ones where a
    cause could move at all."""
    graph = data.draw(graphs())
    target = data.draw(st.sampled_from([one.id for one in graph.propositions]))
    causes = _causes_of(graph, target)
    assume(causes)
    claims = {one.id: one for one in graph.propositions}
    assume(0.05 < claims[target].prior.p < 0.95)
    assume(any(0.0 < claims[one].prior.p < 1.0 for one in causes))

    base = _folded(graph)
    learned = _folded(graph, Observe(target=target, value=True))

    assert any(learned.beliefs[one] != base.beliefs[one] for one in causes)
```

It asserts **"something changed"** — an existential `!=` over a Belief dataclass, at `SMALL = {"versions": 16, "worlds": 4}` (`:64`). No direction, no magnitude, no sign. Observing a positively-linked cause could *lower* its ancestor's probability and this passes. The docstring is candid ("a *capability* claim"), but it is the only ancestor-update test in the file.

The only exact-conditioning check is degenerate: `test_an_observation_forces_the_claim_it_names` (`:1036`) asserts the observed node itself reads exactly `{1.0}` or `{0.0}`. ### Origin marks (●●●) — provenance, three steps out of seven

Defined in `spec/workbench/tiles-ports-wires.md` §"`OriginMark` — provenance at the wire's tail" and repeated identically in `spec/workbench/inspector.md` B4:

| Mark | `provenance` values | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **●●●** | `documented`, `historical`, `market_implied` | "Something was fetched, studied or priced" |
| **●●** | `argued`, `user` | "A mechanism was stated, or a person typed it" |
| **●** | `asserted`, `simulated` | "The model talking, or a probe" |

The rationale, verbatim:

> "Three steps, not seven, because the question a picture can answer is *is there a document behind this, or is it the model talking*. **The exact word is in the Inspector**, drawn by this same component with the word beside it. The mark also carries the exact word as its accessible name, so the seven-way distinction is never lost to a reader who is not looking at the picture."

On placement:

> "The mark sits at the **tail**, where the arrow leaves its cause, and not at the head — the head already carries the arrowhead, and a receipt belongs at the point where the claim was made."

It is one component, `frontend/src/components/OriginMark.tsx`, "drawn by the wire **and** by the Inspector, so the mark and the word can never drift apart" (pinned by INV-workbench.10 and .56).

**Why provenance left the stroke** (`color-motion-type.md`, the cleanest statement of the whole design philosophy):

> "It used to ride the wire's stroke. It cannot any more, because the stroke is fully spent. … A wire cannot be dot-dash because it is an `impulse` and dashed because it is `argued` at the same time; it would be neither, legibly."

This was a live amendment: ADR-0007's original text said "provenance → stroke style (`asserted` dashed)"; the 2026-09-17 amendment (ADR-0007 "More Information" §2) changed it, and `color-motion-type.md` records that `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` UX-6, its INV-12 row, and `spec/workbench/README.md`'s INV-12 row were all rewritten in the same PR.

### Wire stroke — five encodings, none of them colour

`tiles-ports-wires.md` §"The wire, and its five encodings":

| Meaning | Channel | Reads in greyscale |
|---|---|---|
| Signal `shape` | Stroke pattern: `impulse` dot-dash · `step` solid · `ramp` gradient along stroke | Pattern |
| `strength` (unsigned magnitude) | Stroke width, **four steps, not a continuous ramp** (<0.5→1px; 0.5–1.25→2px; 1.25–2.25→3px; ≥2.25→4px) | Width |
| `sustain` vs `trigger` | `sustain` is **double-stroked**; `trigger` single | Doubling |
| `reflexive` | Loops back on itself, carries a **lag chip** in days | The loop |
| `provenance` | Origin mark at the tail | Dot count |

> "**The stroke says one thing and one thing only: what kind of push this is.**"
> "Nothing in that table is a colour. Every wire takes `--text-muted` for its stroke, and a wire's hue says nothing at all."

**The sign trap**, stated three times across chapters because it is the map's live failure mode:

> "The arrow into *Brent settles below $68* is `+1.6` — positive, because it makes that claim come out **true** more often — and the thing the claim describes is a **falling** price. Strength is also read back in **five word bands**, deliberately a different granularity from the four stroke widths: *a faint push toward/against* (<0.25) · *a nudge* (0.25–0.75) · *a clear push* (0.75–1.5) · *a strong push* (1.5–2.5) · *close to decisive / close to ruled out* (≥2.5). "The two granularities differ on purpose and nothing is lost by it, because **the signed number is printed beside the words every time**: `+1.6 · a strong push toward`. ### Probability formatting: `.36`, not `36%`

**What the spec states, with rationale:**

Two significant figures on the number **and on both ends of the range**, always, with the range never dropped. `keyboard-and-access.md` B6 owns the rule for the whole part; `belief.md` gives the why:

> "Precision beyond two figures on an elicited number is a lie about how much we know — the honesty requirement, NFR-1."

> "The chip never drops its range to fit. If the space is too narrow for `.40 (.28–.55)`, the space gets wider — the range does not go. **A number without its range is the fake-precise percentage the whole product is arguing against.**"

Trailing zeros stay: "`.06` prints **`.060`**, because two figures means two figures" — and the stated reason for not special-casing it: "'Two figures except when the second is a zero' would be a second rule for one ugly case."

The certainty guard: "A chip never prints `1.0` and never prints `.0`" — those print `>.99` and `<.01`, on the range's ends too. Why:

> "A likelihood of 1 is a claim that something cannot fail, and this product does not make that claim about the world."

And a worked edge case caught in the spec itself: "JavaScript stores .995 as 0.99499999999999999556, so `(0.995).toPrecision(2)` returns `"0.99"` — under the guard… The formatter must round the decimal value half-up rather than lean on the double."

Rounding happens **once, at paint**: "Round in the view model and you have thrown away precision the Inspector needs; round twice and `.347 → .35 → .4` and now the screen is lying by a whole step." (INV-workbench.37.)

**What the spec does NOT state — a real gap for your review.** There is **no sentence anywhere in `spec/` or `docs/` giving a reason for the decimal form over the percent form.** The `.36` spelling is used ~200 times and never justified. What exists is circumstantial:

- `docs/research/03-ui-ux-directions.md` anti-pattern 4 proposed the opposite: *"**Fake-precise percentages** (\"63.7%\") → round to 5% and show a band: `60% ±15`."* The spec silently rejected both halves — it kept the band, dropped the percent, and swapped 5%-rounding for two-significant-figures. No chapter records that rejection.
- An observable but unstated convention: **percent is reserved for shares and counts, decimals for likelihoods.** The delta rail prints `97%` for the *same direction* column (a share of 2,000 versions); the Inspector's band-share sentence prints `65% of this band is B's own prior`; the outline view speaks "3 per cent" for instrument moves. Likelihoods are always `.36`. Nothing names this rule, so nothing protects it.

`color-motion-type.md` is the shortest workbench chapter (4,193 w) and the most load-bearing.

| Meaning | Channel | Tokens | Redundant non-colour cue |
|---|---|---|---|
| How likely a claim is | Brightness, 5-step **neutral** ramp | `--p-0`…`--p-4` | The number at 2sf with its range |
| Direction of financial effect | Hue: **blue up, amber down** | `--dir-up`, `--dir-down` | A glyph (▲/▼) **and** a sign **and** a word — all three, always |

`hypothesis` — top-left corner cut at 45°, like a flag ("The map starts here; there is exactly one per map") · `event` — plain rectangle · `market` — bottom edge nicked by two semicircles, like a ticket stub ("Something you could actually hold") · `not_tradeable` — right edge open and hairline-dashed ("The map stops here, and nothing leaves").

**The six badge words** (copied from `vocabulary.md`'s Interface words table, "never paraphrased"): **Supposed · date** · **Happened · date** · **Added** · **Retuned** · **Split** · and one derived badge no button produces, **Retracted · date · by "…"**. The six operation code names — `do`, `observe`, `insert`, `retune`, `refine`, `believe` — "never appear on screen."

**Chip states** — four: a number (with the ramp bar behind it); an empty `user` slot rendered as **—** which is a *control* inviting your number; an empty `market` slot reading **no market**; and **no engine yet**. Plus one that replaces the number entirely: while an edit has fixed a claim's value the chip shows **the word** — *Supposed · Oct 1* or *Happened · Oct 1* — "never `1.0`, never `.98` and never `>.99`."

**Two model-chip label variants**, chosen by data (`WorldView.versions` present or absent), not by a flag:
- computed: *"model interval, uncalibrated · how sure we are of `.35` — not how much the world can move"* with a fixed hover sentence about "2 000 versions … eight times in ten. Nobody has checked whether that 8-in-10 holds up".
- stated (everything in this stack): *"stated range · not computed"* / *"This range is stated, not computed — it says how sure the elicitation was. Nothing has worked this number through the map yet."*

**Measured:** width **280 px fixed**; height **content-fit clamped 152–272 px** on the 8px grid, "computed from the content… Never measured from the screen, so layout stays a pure function"; padding 12 px; border one hairline at 10% of text colour; **shadow: None. Not a soft one, not a small one**; radius 6 px.

**Two things explicitly NOT on the tile, with reasons:**
- **No density sparkline.** "a sparkline draws a day-by-day series, and nothing here computes one — a curve shaped by hand would be a picture of numbers nobody worked out." UX-1 keeps it; it arrives with the engine's `series`.
- **Evidence `weight` is not drawn.** "a weight that moves nothing is a number pretending to be an input; it is listed in the Inspector, where it can be labelled for what it is."

A **skeleton tile** is explicitly not a seventh thing: "It is a box, not a claim. It has no identifier on the map, no chips, no kind silhouette, no badge, and no number that could be a number nobody computed."

## 3. The diff view

**The framing question** (`diff-view.md` Purpose):

> "**what did my edit reach, and what did it provably leave alone?**"

**Two-world compare — one layout, two paintings (B1).** Lay out the *union* of both worlds once, then paint twice into that one coordinate space: **A′** at full opacity and solid, **A** at **20% opacity, dashed**, behind it. "Nothing moves between them, so every difference you see is a real difference and not a re-layout." Anti-pattern 3: "Do not lay out A and A′ separately and place them side by side… two layouts mean every tile moves a little, and a reader cannot tell a real change from a layout change."

**Ghost values.** In this stack **there are none, deliberately**:

> "**For the second world, before the engine, there is no second set of numbers at all.** No committed illustrative world, no hand-written likelihoods, no 'illustrative numbers' chip. A number nobody computed is exactly the state a reader cannot trace."

So the answer is **structural**, four states derived from the branch alone: `added` (solid + accent ring) · `killed` (ghosted, struck through, desaturated — and `killed` means *forced false*, full stop) · `downstream` (drawn live, number slot reading "no engine yet") · `untouched` (neutral). A fifth, `shifted`, "needs two numbers to compare, so it cannot exist here" — INV-workbench.44 forbids producing it without two numbers.

Opacity composes: the hover lens **multiplies** the ghost's 20% rather than replacing it, "so a tile that is both off the hovered path and old lands near 3% and disappears — which is correct: you asked to see one path in one world."

**A ⇄ A′ is `Space`, a hard switch, never a crossfade.** "Two half-drawn worlds on top of each other is a picture of nothing, and a crossfade invites the eye to read the blur as a number moving." Scrubbable; under reduced motion "there is nothing to remove, because there was never a tween."

**The delta rail.** With the engine, a row reads:

```
M1  A Polymarket contract "Brent below $70 on 2026-10-31" resolves YES.
    tradeable
    down · largest on 2026-10-04
    .50 ▼ .42        .27        97%
```

Three columns: the change, **how firm** (`rangeWidth`), **same direction** (`agreement`). "The chevron sits between the two readings rather than after them, so the row reads as one number becoming another, and the direction is a word as well as a glyph because a glyph read aloud is nothing at all."

Ranking = size of the move × **the weakest arrow on the best-backed route** from any edit to that ending — "the route whose weakest arrow is strongest. Two factors and no more." The two side columns are **never folded into the rank** (INV-workbench.47): "Folding width into the rank would sink exactly the claims that most deserve attention."

An ending that did not move gets a **greyed row reading *no change***, never a missing one — decided 2026-09-17, closing `multiverse/diff.md` open question 5, "because a reader looking at that list alone cannot tell *'it did not move'* from *'it is not on this map'*." And the verdict is read off the engine's `ClaimDiff.state`, never derived in the browser: "that would be the browser re-running the shifted test, with its own .005 floor and its own 90% bar, and two answers to that question is one too many."

Before the engine the rail prints map order with `no engine yet` in every slot: "**A rail that invented an ordering would be inventing the one thing the rail exists to tell you** — map order is visibly arbitrary and says so; a fabricated ranking looks like an answer."

**The hero of the diff is the claim that did NOT move.** This is stated outright and is the most distinctive UX idea in the corpus:

> "> **R — *OPEC+ announces output restraint* — is `untouched`. Nothing on this branch can reach it.**
>
> R's only incoming arrow is B → R, the **feedback** arrow… So the screen can say out loud: *your strike moves the oil price, the insurance premium, both contracts and the diplomatic ending — and it cannot move OPEC's announcement.* **That sentence is the product**, and `INV-workbench.41` and `.42` below pin it."

**The branch panel** lists edits in the order they were made, each with its badge: "Read as a sequence, the rule that a later addition outranks an earlier supposition is obvious; met as a number that moved on its own, it reads as a bug." Append-only: "an audit trail you can edit is not one."

## 4. The Inspector

**One persistent side panel, three subjects** (`InspectorProps.subject`): `{kind:"claim"}` · `{kind:"link"}` · `{kind:"generation"}` · or `null` ("Nothing selected is a real state with its own copy, not a blank panel"). There are **no pop-ups anywhere in this product** (UX-10, INV-workbench.50).

### The claim panel — B1's literal render order

```
<claim sentence>                                          <kind>
RESOLVES      criteria / judged by / by <date>
BASE RATE     reference class, k of n, sources — or "no reference class recorded"
PRIOR         .28 (.15–.42)          model
BELIEFS       model / user / market, each on one line, plus the stated-or-computed
              label and its hover sentence under the model row
EVIDENCE      claim, address, direction, weight
WHY THIS NUMBER   the decomposition — or "no engine yet"
[reserved band slot]  stack 06, renders nothing here
[path-product bar]
```

- **Resolution triple is never optional** — criteria, adjudicating source, date, on every claim (INV-1, INV-workbench.58): "a claim nobody can score is not a claim."
- **Three voices, never merged** (INV-11 / INV-workbench.52). "**Say which source a number came from before calling the gap an edge**: the gap is only worth trading once the engine has written the model's half of it."
- **The decomposition** = prior, one line per incoming arrow with its push and its reason, then the result. Three rules: one line per incoming arrow the world carries, not a selection; no line may be a number whose owner cannot be named; "**This panel never computes the block.** A canvas that added up its own pushes would be a second engine, and two engines disagree." Whole block or none — "A block missing its last line reads as a sum somebody forgot to finish, and the reader cannot tell that from a sum that went wrong."
- **One fixed sentence for reweighting**, word for word: *"this claim moved only because the observation made some versions count more."* Rendered exactly when the engine's diff row carries `movedOnlyByReweighting`, "and by no other route: no comparison of a same-direction share against zero, no check for whether a claim has incoming arrows, no inference from an empty decomposition."
- **The reserved band slot** (stack 06): will read *"**65% of this band is B's own prior; pin that down and the band goes from 30 points to 12.**"* — "the honest answer to *where should I spend the next hour of research*". Today: "leaves the slot in place, leaves a comment in the component naming `range_shares`… and **renders nothing** — not a placeholder sentence, not a spinner, not a greyed-out example."
- **The path-product bar (INV-8)**: the multiplied-out likelihood of one route's steps, on the **best-backed route** (weakest arrow strongest; ties go to the shorter). "A chain of four plausible steps is not a plausible chain, and the product is the number that says so." Three distinct readings that must never stand in for each other: the number · `no path shown` · *no path from the hypothesis reaches this claim any more*. "The bar never disappears; a missing bar looks like a bar nobody needed." And the wart is printed, not hidden: the factors "are each read on their **own resolve-by day** — H by Nov 1, B by Oct 15, M1 by Oct 31 — so the product multiplies numbers read on three different days, and not even in order… **it is not a joint probability**."

### Yes — there is a full edge/wire inspector

`inspector.md` B4, seven fields in fixed order (`LinkDetail` = `LinkView` "with nothing added and nothing left out"):

```
<source claim>   →   <target claim>
WHY        the rationale/mechanism in prose
PUSH       +1.6 — a strong push toward
KIND       trigger — a domino: it fires once…  /  sustain — the desk holding the apple
DELAY      2 days from the strait opening
OVER TIME  impulse — a one-time spike, half gone after 30 days
SOURCES    title / host · fetched: —  nobody fetched this; a person put the address in
WHERE IT CAME FROM   ●● argued — the model stated a mechanism, and no retrieval step has run
```

"**Mode is a sentence, not a word to look up.**" `fetched` is "the day our own retrieval step pulled the page down" — a source with no retrieval day "is never rendered as though it had one" (INV-workbench.59).

### Fields you asked about

- **mechanism** — yes, the `WHY` section on the link panel (`rationale`).
- **evidence** — yes, `EvidenceView` with claim, address, direction and weight; weight is listed here and deliberately not drawn on the tile.
- **sources** — yes, on links, with per-source `retrieved: Known<string>`.
- **provenance** — yes, mark + exact word of the seven, one shared `OriginMark`.
- **counter-argument** — **no such field exists.** The closest things: evidence `direction: 1 | -1` (a `−` clipping "cuts against the claim"); negative-strength arrows read as *a push against*; and the **refusal strip / transcript**, which quotes every proposal the validator turned down. `docs/research/03-ui-ux-directions.md` cites FutureSearch's "competing YES thesis / competing NO thesis" agents and `02-causal-modeling-formalisms.md` ranks an "adversarial critique pass" fourth for calibration ROI — neither is specified into the UI.
- **"falsified if"** — **specified as missing.** Inspector open question 1, verbatim: *"**Where does 'falsified if' come from?** FR-10 lists it among the panel's contents and no field on a claim carries it: the resolution criteria read backwards, or a genuinely missing field on `Proposition`. **Owner:** `spec/graph/proposition.md`."* The research doc's mock-up shows a `FALSIFIED IF · strike <72h` block; the spec has no field for it. **This is an open UX hole.**

### The third subject: the generation (B7)

`THIS GENERATION` prints the receipt field by field — model, calls, tokens in, tokens out, read from cache, web searches, cost, took, mode (`replay · recorded <date> · prompt <hash>`) — and "the panel adds nothing up. It does not total the two token counts, does not work a cost out of a token count and a price, and does not time anything." Then `TRANSCRIPT`, with **three** kinds of line: `accepted`, `refused` (quoting the model verbatim plus the validator's own sentence per rule broken), and `stopped` — "the one a reader would otherwise never see." A stopped line carries no `at`, "so the positions in this list have gaps in them, and the gaps are the stops."

## 5. Keyboard grammar and a11y announcements

**Elaborate in depth, small in surface: 10 bindings, 2 announcement sentences, 7 spoken outline items.**

The entire key map (`keyboard-and-access.md`, "UX-9, the whole of it"):

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `⌘K` | command palette |
| `j` / `k` | next / previous sibling **in the column you are in** |
| `h` / `l` | back / forward **along a wire** (toward causes / effects) |
| `E` | intervene — opens the six-button panel on the focused claim |
| `B` | fork a branch from here |
| `Space` | A ⇄ A′, a hard switch |
| `?` | shortcuts sheet |
| `Escape` | close top overlay |

The design work is concentrated in `h`/`l`, which is the chapter's stated centrepiece ("This is the part that matters"):

- Movement follows **wires, not geometry**. "Pressing `l` on B and landing on a tile to your left is correct" — because `B → R` is a feedback arrow pointing back into column 1.
- **Feedback wires count for navigation but not for the diff**, under one rule written once in `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` and cited by four chapters: *"The map the engine works through is the map with feedback arrows set aside. Anything that asks **what can move** reads that map — the affected set, diff states, propagation's ordering, layering. Anything that asks **what can I walk to** reads the whole map — the hover lens, `h`/`l`, the outline."*
- **Disambiguation when several wires leave a tile**: the step lands on the neighbour nearest the focused tile's own vertical position, "and the *others* become the `j`/`k` set at the tile you arrive on — so `h` then `j` reaches any of them in two keystrokes and nothing on the map is unreachable." The rejected alternative is named: "A chooser overlay listing the wires was the alternative, and it is a pop-up in all but name."
- **No wrapping** on `j`/`k`: "wrapping quietly teleports you to the top and you lose your place." Status line says *"last claim in this column"* rather than beeping.
- A **status line** under the canvas names what the last keystroke did, including which wire you took: *"along the feedback arrow · 14 days"*.

**Overlays vs dialogs (B4)** — four conditions that make the palette honest under a no-modals promise: nothing waits on them; the canvas stays live with no scrim; `Escape` always closes; neither is ever the only route to anything. The honest tension is left open: whether the palette's focus ring is declared `aria-modal="true"` — "putting the word 'modal' in our accessibility tree while the product's copy says there are no modals is uncomfortable."

**Announcements — exactly two sentences, and the *today* one is the interesting one.** An `aria-live="polite"` region speaks one line when a branch re-propagates.

Once the engine is connected:
> *"Branch created. Six claims changed, one retracted."*

Today, because nothing has computed a change:
> *"Branch created. One claim added, six claims your edit can reach, one supposition retracted. No numbers yet."*

> "Saying 'six claims changed' would be inventing exactly the state the second veto exists to stop… Every count comes from somewhere nameable… and **no numbers yet** said out loud rather than left as a silence. When `ApiWorldSource` lands, 'your edit can reach' becomes 'changed' and the count becomes a computed one. Nothing is deleted at that point, because nothing false was said."

**The outline view (B7)** is the deepest a11y work. `role="tree"`, built **from the world, never from what is on screen**. "A map is not a tree", so it is a spanning tree: one item per claim at first arrival, and a claim with several causes "does not appear twice — instead its sentence names every incoming wire." Mode and sign arrive as words: `trigger` → **caused by**, `sustain` → **held up by**, negative strength → **pushed the other way by**. The chapter then writes out **all seven Hormuz claims as spoken sentences**, e.g.:

> **B** — *"Brent crude settles below $68 for five sessions. Model .28, range .15 to .42. Caused by the strait reopening, two days later. Held up by the war-risk premium falling. Pushed the other way by OPEC+ restraint. Three claims follow."*

A claim hidden behind a "+n more" tile still gets an outline item, and activating "+n more" **opens this view filtered to that column** — a reuse decision, not a new surface.

Focus: `--focus` measures 12.1:1 dark / 5.7:1 light. "`outline: none` appears nowhere in the tree" and anti-pattern 10 is "**Do not write `outline: none`**, anywhere, for any reason."

Nine invariants, INV-workbench.31–.39. Four open questions, all honest (`aria-modal`; `j`/`k` wrapping; whether focus movement is announced — "whether that line is also an `aria-live` region, or whether that would be unbearable chatter, is untested"; how the outline is reached).

## 6. Layout and zoom

**Layout:** ELK layered, five options and no others, pinned by INV-workbench.20:

```ts
"elk.algorithm": "layered",
"elk.direction": "RIGHT",
"elk.layered.nodePlacement.strategy": "NETWORK_SIMPLEX",
"elk.layered.crossingMinimization.semiInteractive": "true",
"elk.layered.spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers": "120",
```

Plus `elk.position` set **per tile** — "how an already-placed tile says where it wants to stay." ELK says *layer*; "On screen and in this chapter the word is **column**, because that is what a reader sees." Runs in a **Web Worker**; `elkjs` is imported by the worker file and nothing else (INV-workbench.21).

**Base map: four columns** — `0: H` · `1: C · N1 · R` · `2: B` · `3: M1 · M2`. **Union with the strike branch: five columns**, and the chapter names the consequence rather than hiding it: "**Read that against B1 and notice what happened: every base claim moved one column right.** It had to." The mitigation is honest too — the shift is a rigid 400-px translation, `setCenter` on the focused tile makes it invisible, and "**creating a claim moves focus to it**." Pinning columns was rejected because "S would have to stay where the base map had nothing, which puts a cause to the right of its effect."

**Semantic zoom — one rule, two derived thresholds.** This is the strongest piece of reasoning in the chapter:

> "The rule: **no text ever lands below 11 pixels on the glass.** There is no counter-scaling anywhere — a tile at 0.7 zoom really is drawn at 0.7, text and all — so the thresholds are arithmetic, not taste"

| Consequence | Sum | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Summary below ≈ **0.85** zoom | 11 ÷ 13 = 0.846… | a full tile's smallest type is `--text-sm`, 13 px |
| Zoom floor **0.5** | 11 ÷ 22 = 0.5 | a summary tile's type is `--text-lg`, 22 px |

> "**This supersedes the 0.6 threshold in the plan and in decision record 0007, dated 2026-09-17.** 0.6 was a chosen number; 0.846 is a derived one, and deriving it is what makes the 11-pixel promise true rather than approximately true."

**Two detail tiers built, three named.** UX-4's rungs: **Near** = full tile with evidence (≥0.85) · **Mid** = the summary tile — claim + three belief chips **inside the same kind silhouette**, nothing else (0.5–0.85) · **Far** = worlds and their terminal deltas — "**Not this stack.** It needs several worlds side by side (FR-17)." The silhouette never goes: "dropping it would lose the claim's kind at exactly the zoom where you are scanning for one."

**The honest cost, measured and printed:** "on a 1440-pixel-wide window the first frame is summary tiles, because `fitView` cannot fit the map any larger. At 1600 wide it is full tiles, at about 11.4 pixels — legible, and only just. A narrow window therefore opens on summaries and you zoom in to read. That is the price of the promise."

**Density cap:** seven tiles per column, then **"+n more"** — the first seven in ELK's own within-column order ("so nothing new has to be ranked"), and the rest open the filtered outline. "A collapsed claim's wires do not disappear… The wires of the hidden claims attach to the '+n more' tile" (how they bundle is open question 1).

**Framing:** `fitView` exactly once on open; `setCenter` on the focused tile thereafter. **No tile is draggable** — "Not 'mostly', not 'except the ones you pinned' — none, anywhere" — and the shortcuts sheet says so out loud, because "Nobody should have to discover this by failing."

**Reflexive arrows are removed before layering** and put back for drawing: "The loop is real, it is on screen, and it takes no part in deciding who sits where."

**A self-declared red flag (B9, open question 4):** NFR-7 says 60 tiles render and re-layout in under 100 ms, but `elapsedMs` measures ELK alone and ADR-0007 already puts ELK at 50–150 ms on 60 nodes. "So the test may land as a **known-red pin** that records the real figure rather than as a passing check."
